content.conclusion:
In this paper, we introduce a novel framework to evaluate the cost pass-through of imported crop
pricesinasmallopeneconomy,andempiricallymeasurethedegreeofsuchcosttransmissionusing
the case of South Korea. Our framework demonstrates that the direction of markup adjustments in
response to import price shocks depends on firms’ cost structures (i.e., the degree of dependence of
imported inputs) and market structure, such as product differentiation and demand curvature
(Ritz,2024;St-Pierre,2023;Weyl&Fabinger,2013).Specifically,wecategorizefirmsbyforeigncrop
dependence and demand curvature to illustrate differing markup responses. Recognizing that firm
size is also a key determinant of markup adjustment (Amiti et al., 2019), partially accounting for
demandproperties,weclassifyfirmsbasedonboththeirsizeanddegreeofforeigncropdependence.
Furthermore, building on DLW, we develop an empirical approach to estimating cost pass-through
elasticitiesthatcapturesheterogeneousmarkupadjustmentsacrossfirmtypes.
Our findings reveal an increasing polarization in the markup distribution, driven by growth
among higher percentile groups. Also, we identify heterogeneous markup elasticities across firm
types and sectors, providing a nuanced understanding of strategic pricing with respect to imported
crop prices. Notably, firms that rely heavily on imported crops have shown declining pass-through
over time, while firms less or not reliant on foreign crops have increasingly raised their pass-
throughrates.Thesepatternssuggestthatmorefirmsthatdonotdirectlyreceiveimportcostshocks
engageinstrategicmarkupadjustments,underscoringtheimportanceofanalyzingequilibriumpass-
throughfrommultipleangles.
Finally, we note both strengths and caveats of our approach relative to conventional time-series
pass-through measurements.By explicitly using estimated firm-level markups, our method not only
reveals micro-level markup adjustments and pass-throughs but also facilitates extrapolation to pre-
dict the first-order approximation of inflationary effects from import price shocks. This feature is
particularly useful for short-term simulations,as demonstrated inthe model validation. Building on
this, a promising avenue for future research would be to apply our framework to a narrower set of
complementary sectors, exploring how a shock to one firm type propagates cross-sector spillovers
via complementary pricing. However, caution is warranted in applying our approach to long-run
dynamics,asitdoesnotcapturetheintertemporalstoragebehaviorofmaterialinputs.
